content.text: I want to start work on SYS-586 next, but I think this goes wider. What's best practice when it comes to component versus page layout design? How much responsibility should rest with the page to lay out components - presumably the idea should be that components should be easily re-usable in different contexts as appropriate and also Storybook's involvement means the components need to be testable and snapshottable sensibly on their own.

Good context from SYS-586 — the ticket itself already surfaces the exact issue: wrapping `SignIn` in `<Paper>` at the *page* level broke because tests render pages without a `MantineProvider`, and had to be patched around rather than fixing the actual architecture.

My recommendation: split it by what the wrapper is *for*, not by convenience.

- **Container (width/measure)** is a page-layout concern — it's about how a page arranges its content on the screen, not what the component *is*. Pages should own it, ideally via `<Container size="sm">` etc. using Mantine's theme sizes instead of ad hoc `maw="35rem"` — that's literally what SYS-586 is asking for.
- **Paper/Card (chrome — elevation, border, background)** is usually part of a component's own visual identity, not something imposed by context. If a component looks "broken" without its Paper wrapper regardless of where it's placed, the Paper belongs *inside* the component, not bolted on at the page. That's why the SignIn/Paper test breakage was a smell: it meant a presentational detail of the component leaked into the page, forcing every consumer (including tests and Storybook) to know about a dependency that should've been internal.

The tradeoff: pushing chrome into components risks double-wrapping if a component is later composed inside another Paper/Card, and pages lose some flexibility to vary presentation per context. Mitigate that by making chrome conditional via a prop (e.g. `withBorder`/`padded` defaulting sensibly) rather than hardcoding it, and always render the component standalone in Storybook so double-wrapping is visually obvious immediately.

Practical test for each existing case: **can this component be dropped into a Storybook story or a `.vitest.spec.tsx` render with nothing but `MantineProvider` and still look/behave correctly?** If not, whatever's missing (Paper, Card, spacing) should move inside the component. Want me to survey the codebase for current `maw=` and page-level `<Paper>`/`<Card>` usages to scope how big SYS-586 actually is before you commit to it?

Yes. I guess that really I need to take SYS-584 together with this, since I'm almost certainly going the wrong way by not using Container for layout on the player profile page. Possibly I can get rid of any lingering use of container queries

## 2. Existing `<Container>` usage

**35 usages**, `size` prop distribution:

8 page.tsx files:

- `src/app/footy/tables/page.tsx:16` — `<Paper p="xl" withBorder>` wraps a static `<List>` of table links (no sub-component; markup lives entirely in the page).
- `src/app/footy/response/page.tsx:60` — `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` wraps `<GameInvitationResponseForm>`.
- `src/app/footy/admin/page.tsx:24` — `<Paper w="100%" p="xl">` (inside `Container size="xs"`) wraps a `<Flex>` of two admin widgets (`AdminUpdatePlayerRecords`, `AdminExportAuth`).
- `src/app/footy/countrymap/page.tsx:23` — `<Paper p="xl">` wraps a `<Title>`, descriptive `<Text>`, and `<PlayerCountryMap>`.
- `src/app/footy/forgottenpassword/page.tsx:12` — `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` wraps `<ForgottenPasswordForm>`.
- `src/app/footy/auth/signin/page.tsx:18` — `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` wraps `<SignIn>`.
- `src/app/footy/auth/claim/[token]/page.tsx:55` — `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` wraps `<ClaimSignup>` (has the TODO noted above).
- `src/app/footy/admin/newgame/page.tsx:16-18` — `<Container size="sm">` wraps `<Paper p="xl">` which wraps `<Title>` + `<NewGameForm>`.

No `<Card` usage was found at page level anywhere; the only `<Card` usage in the whole codebase is inside a component: `src/components/ResponsesForm/ResponsesForm.tsx:199-200`.

Pattern: the `maw="35rem"` + `Paper` combo is repeated identically across 4 page files (signin, forgottenpassword, claim, response) purely to wrap a single form component — a strong candidate for either a shared page-level layout wrapper or moving the `Paper`/width constraint inside each form component (mirroring `PasswordResetForm.tsx`, which already puts the same `Paper maw="35rem"` chrome *inside* the component rather than the page).

## 4. CSS container queries (`@container`, `container-type`, `containerType`, `useContainerQuery`)

- **`src/components/PlayerCard/PlayerCard.module.css:9`** — `.imageContainer { container-type: inline-size; }`, explicitly commented (lines 5-7) as establishing "a query container so the badges/trophies below can size themselves as a proportion of the mugshot's own rendered width."
- **`src/components/PlayerCard/PlayerCard.module.css:19`** — `.badges { max-width: 30cqw; ... }` — consumes the container query unit.
- No literal `@container` at-rule, no `containerType` (camelCase JS), and no `useContainerQuery` hook exist anywhere in the codebase.
- **However**, the `cqw` (container-query-width) unit is used extensively downstream, all sized relative to the `.imageContainer` established in PlayerCard:
  - `src/components/CountryFlag/CountryFlag.tsx:9` (doc comment) / `CountryFlag.vitest.spec.tsx:9`
  - `src/components/ClubBadge/ClubBadge.tsx:9` (doc comment) / `ClubBadge.vitest.spec.tsx:11`
  - `src/components/PlayerCountries/PlayerCountries.tsx:14,19`
  - `src/components/PlayerClubs/PlayerClubs.tsx:14,19`
  - `src/components/PlayerTrophies/PlayerTrophies.tsx:20,35-36`
  - `src/components/PlayerTrophyTally/PlayerTrophyTally.tsx:17 (doc), 46` and its spec file (many instances)
- Also worth noting separately: **Mantine's `<Grid type="container">`** in `src/components/PlayerProfile/PlayerProfile.tsx:68` and `:95` uses Mantine's own container-query-based responsive grid (with custom `breakpoints={{ xs: '24em', sm: '36em', md: '54em', lg: '74em', xl: '88em' }}` at line 96) — this is a distinct mechanism from the CSS `container-type` above, but conceptually related (container-relative responsiveness rather than viewport-relative). Not found used anywhere else in the codebase.

These two container-query systems (PlayerCard's CSS `container-type`/`cqw` chain, and PlayerProfile's Mantine `Grid type="container"`) are self-contained/local sizing mechanisms for element-relative responsiveness within cards — distinct from the page-level `maw`/`Container` width-constraint concern SYS-586 targets, but they do sit inside the exact component tree (PlayerProfile → PlayerCard → PlayerCountries/PlayerClubs/PlayerTrophies) that SYS-584 is about, so worth being aware of so the refactor doesn't disturb them.

## 5. Player profile page — current top-level layout structure

Route: `src/app/footy/player/[id]/page.tsx` (there's also a legacy redirect shim at `src/app/footy/player/[id]/[year]/page.tsx` that 301s `/player/[id]/[year]` → `/player/[id]?year=[year]`).

Structure, outside-in:

1. **`CustomAppShell.tsx`** (global, applies to every page) → `AppShell.Main` → `<Container fluid p="xl">` (no max-width, just padding).
2. **`src/app/footy/layout.tsx`** — segment layout, adds only `<SearchParamErrorNotification />`, no layout/width markup.
3. **`page.tsx`** (`PlayerPage`, server component) — does data-fetching only; renders `<AutoRefresh>` + `<PlayerProfile ...>` inside a bare fragment (`<>...</>`). **No `Container`, `Paper`, or width constraint at the page level at all.**
4. **`src/components/PlayerProfile/PlayerProfile.tsx`** — the actual layout lives here:
   - Root: `<Stack gap="sm" w="100%">` — full width, no max-width, no wrapping `Paper`/`Container`.
   - Row 1: `<Grid type="container" mb="lg" gap="xs" align="center">` with 3 `GridCol`s — prev-player arrow (`span="content"`), centered `<TitleWithYearDropdown>` (`span="auto"`), next-player arrow (`span="content"`).
   - Row 2: `<Grid type="container" breakpoints={{...}}>` with 4 `GridCol`s (`span={{ base: 12, sm: 6, lg: 3 }}`) each containing one card-style component: `PlayerCard`, `PlayerInfo`, `PlayerResults`, `PlayerPositions`.
   - Row 3: `<Group>` wrapping a single `<Paper p="sm" w="auto" withBorder style={{ flex: '1' }}>` containing `<PlayerHeatmap>`.

So the "wrong way" this ticket likely refers to: the page renders **full-bleed** (only constrained by the app-shell's `fluid` container plus its own `padding` prop), with **no `<Container size="...">`** anywhere in the profile's own tree to cap line-length/card-grid width on ultra-wide screens, while several *other, simpler* pages (signin, forgottenpassword, response, claim, tables, countrymap, admin) instead hard-code ad hoc `maw="35rem"` Paper wrappers directly in the page file rather than using `Container`. The player profile page is essentially the "no constraint" case; the auth/form pages are the "informal maw constraint in the page" case — SYS-586 appears aimed at reconciling both onto `<Container size="...">`, and SYS-584 at deciding whether the `Paper`/chrome (`PlayerHeatmap`'s wrapping `Paper`, or the grid-of-cards on the profile) belongs in `PlayerProfile.tsx` (page-adjacent) vs. pushed down into the leaf components themselves.

## 6. Mantine theme file (`src/theme.ts`)

Full contents (13 lines):
```ts
import {
    createTheme,
} from '@mantine/core';

export const theme = createTheme({
    components: {
        Paper: {
            defaultProps: {
                shadow: 'xl',
            },
        },
    },
});
```

- No `Container` size overrides, no custom breakpoints, no spacing/width scale defined — only a single `Paper` default prop (`shadow: 'xl'`) is customized.
- **No existing "standard sizes" constants** (no `theme.other`, no exported width/size tokens) anywhere in `theme.ts` or elsewhere that a refactor could reuse — any `Container` size standardization (e.g. mapping the informal `35rem` to a Mantine size token, or adding custom `Container` sizes via `createTheme`) would be new work, not an extension of something already there.</result>

The survey confirms the hunch, and it turns out you left yourself a note about this back in `claim/[token]/page.tsx:19-22` — literally the origin of SYS-586. Here's what's actually going on:

**The `maw="35rem"` pattern (SYS-586 core)**
Four pages (`signin`, `forgottenpassword`, `auth/claim/[token]`, `response`) each hard-code an identical `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` wrapper directly in the page file around a single form component. One component, `PasswordResetForm`, already does it differently — it puts that exact same `Paper maw="35rem"` wrapper *inside itself* rather than making its page do it. That's the precedent to standardize on. Bonus: `35rem` (560px) is almost exactly Mantine's built-in `Container size="xs"` (540px/33.75rem) — so this isn't a case for inventing custom theme tokens, it's a case for using the size scale Mantine already ships and currently isn't consistently used (usage today is Container `size` scattered across `xs/sm/md/lg/xl/fluid` with no obvious rule).

**Player profile / SYS-584**
`PlayerProfile.tsx` has no `Container` or max-width anywhere — it's a bare `<Stack w="100%">`, only constrained by `CustomAppShell`'s `<Container fluid p="xl">`, which imposes padding but no cap. That's exactly why zooming out lets the mugshot and card grid stretch to fill the viewport. Two unrelated mechanisms already live in that same tree and must be left alone: `PlayerCard`'s CSS `container-type: inline-size` (element-relative badge sizing via `cqw`) and `PlayerProfile`'s Mantine `<Grid type="container">` (its own internal responsive breakpoints). Neither is a page-width concern — SYS-586/584 shouldn't touch them.

**Proposed plan:**
1. Fix `PlayerProfile`'s missing width cap first (SYS-584) — wrap it in `<Container size="xl">` at the `page.tsx` level (page owns width; `PlayerProfile` stays layout-agnostic of the page, consistent with it being reusable/storybook-testable on its own).
2. For SYS-586, migrate the four `maw="35rem"` pages: move the `Paper` chrome into each form component (mirroring `PasswordResetForm`), drop the page-level `Paper`/`maw`, replace with `<Container size="xs">` where a wrapper is still needed. Delete the now-resolved TODO comment.
3. Leave `PlayerCard`/`PlayerProfile`'s container-query and `Grid type="container"` usage untouched.
4. Audit the other one-off `maw` values (`Turnout` 24rem, `PlayerProfileForm` 32rem, `InvoiceForm` 30rem, `WinnersTable`/`RecordsTable` 24rem, `EnquiryForm` 520px) case by case — decide per-component whether they map onto the Mantine scale or are legitimately bespoke.

Want me to proceed in that order, starting with the player profile fix (SYS-584) since it's already marked In Progress?

content.text:
**Root cause found and fixed.** It wasn't related to today's SYS-584/586 work — it was a regression from yesterday's commit `297ab1c9` ("SYS-594 Standardise on dot notation for table subcomponents").

That commit changed several components from standalone imports (`TableTr`, `TableTd`, etc.) to Mantine's dot-notation (`Table.Tr`, `Table.Td`). That's safe in Client Components, but four of the affected files — `PlayerInfo`, `PlayerResults`, `PlayerPositions`, `PlayerArse` — are Server Components (no `'use client'`). Under this stack (Next.js 16 + Turbopack), Mantine's compound static properties (`Table.Tbody`, `Table.Tr`, etc.) don't survive the RSC server/client serialization boundary, so they resolved to `undefined` at render time — hence "Element type is invalid: undefined." Client Components like `Turnout`, `WinnersTable`, and `RecordsTable` were unaffected because they never cross that boundary.

I confirmed this by bisecting the actual component tree on a from-scratch dev server (cache cleared, fresh process) rather than guessing from stack traces, which were too generic to pinpoint anything.

**Fix:** reverted just those four files to the standalone named imports (`TableTbody`/`TableTr`/`TableTh`/`TableTd`), leaving the dot-notation standardization intact everywhere it's actually safe (Client Components). Verified clean on players 1, 2, 3, and 201 on a completely fresh dev server, and `typecheck`/`lint`/`knip`/full component+page test suites (683 + 236 tests) all still pass.

**Takeaway for future work:** Mantine's dot-notation compound components (`Table.Tr`, `Table.Th`, etc.) are only safe in Client Components in this codebase — Server Components should keep using the standalone named imports. Worth a note in CLAUDE.md if you want to prevent this recurring.

Compound components are throwing "Element type is invalid" errors in Next.js 15.5.5, where the error states the component received undefined instead of a proper component reference. ## Common Causes

The error typically occurs due to:

1. **Export/Import Issues**: You likely forgot to export your component from the file it's defined in, or you might have mixed up default and named imports.

2. **Version Mismatches**: For Mantine specifically, this error can occur if you don't have the correct version of Mantine or Tabler Icons installed, and you should make sure all mantine packages are at least v7.3 and that the @tabler/icons-react package is at least v2.23.0.

3. **Turbopack-Specific Issues**: Turbopack has shown issues where it's unable to load certain resources, resulting in the same "Element type is invalid" error, though the issue works without the --turbo flag.

The most relevant GitHub issue appears to be in the Next.js repository (#84961), which specifically documents compound components failing with this error in recent versions.

Thank you for the report!

To explain why this is the case: when a server component imports a client component, it receives a special client reference that the RSC runtime knows how to send to the browser. In other words, you aren't receiving the underlying export, it's only used to be passed to the client. 

This is described a bit here: https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client:
> When a server evaluated module imports values from a 'use client' module, the values must either be a React component or [supported serializable prop values](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#passing-props-from-server-to-client-components) to be passed to a Client Component. Any other use case will throw an exception

However, I think the error itself can be improved here. React actually has a special message for this case which should read something like:

> Error: Cannot access <module> on the server. You cannot dot into a client module from a server component. You can only pass the imported name through.

We will investigate why it's not being shown in this particular case.

### Describe the bug

Been trying to get Drawer to work within a storybook.  Followed the docs, but continue to get the error:

```
Element type is invalid: expected a string (for built-in components) or a class/function (for composite components) but got: undefined
```

The drawer works fine when used in a reduced test case sandbox, but the following code, as reduced as possible does not.

```typescript
// panel.tsx
import { Drawer, Button, Card, Text } from "@mantine/core";
import { useDisclosure } from "@mantine/hooks";
import * as React from "react";

export interface PanelProps {
	isOpened?: boolean;
}

export function Panel (props: PanelProps) {
	const {
		isOpened = true,
	} = props;

content.text:
Yes — this is a known, confirmed issue in the Next.js RSC architecture, not something specific to Mantine or this codebase.

**`vercel/next.js#84961`** — "Compound components are throwing Error: Element type is invalid in next 15.5.5" — is essentially the exact same bug: a compound sub-component (`Tabs.Tab` in their repro, `Table.Tr` in ours) logs as `undefined` when accessed from a Server Component, but as a real function from inside the component's own client module. A Next.js maintainer confirmed the fix is making the accessing component `'use client'` and linked to the fuller explanation.

**`vercel/next.js#75192`** has the actual root-cause explanation from a Next.js team member (`ztanner`): when a Server Component imports a `'use client'` module, it only receives an opaque **client reference** for passing to the browser — not the real export — so you cannot "dot into" a sub-property of it (`Table.Tr`) from server code; you can only pass the named import straight through as a component. React has a dedicated, clearer error for this ("Cannot access `<module>` on the server...") but Next.js isn't consistently surfacing it, which is why we saw the generic "Element type is invalid: undefined" instead — that gap is acknowledged but still open, and a commenter notes there are "numerous issues on the topic" (referencing `#76000`).

So: not a bug in Mantine's `Table` itself, and not fixable via a Mantine or Next.js update — it's an inherent constraint of the current RSC model. The correct pattern (matching what we just restored) is what Mantine's own docs and the linked writeup recommend: Server Components must use the standalone named exports (`TableTr`, `TableTd`, etc.), reserving the dot-notation (`Table.Tr`) for Client Components only.

Sources:
- [Compound components are throwing Error: Element type is invalid in next 15.5.5 (#84961)](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/84961)
- [RSC dot-notation explanation (#75192)](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/75192)
- [Multipart namespace components: addressing RSC and dot-notation issues](https://ivicabatinic.from.hr/posts/multipart-namespace-components-addressing-rsc-and-dot-notation-issues)
Stash the changes which are not related to this fix: I'll come back to them

content.text:
Before doing the bulk conversion, I hit one genuine blocker worth flagging: `@mantine/tiptap`'s `RichTextEditorToolbar` (used as `RichTextEditor.Toolbar` in `RichTextMailBody.tsx` and `SendEmailForm.tsx`) has **no public standalone export** — its package `exports` map only exposes the package root, and the toolbar component only exists as a static property on `RichTextEditor`. Every other dot-notation usage in the codebase (Table, AppShell, Popover, ScrollArea, Progress, Menu, and all the other RichTextEditor controls) does have a real standalone named export I can switch to.

Note this specific case is actually safe today regardless — both files using it are already `'use client'`, so the RSC boundary bug can't bite them. But it can't be converted to a plain import since Mantine doesn't ship one.

options.label: Add a small client-side compat wrapper

57	## Architecture & Layers
58	
59	- **Pages:** `src/app/footy/**` — Next.js App Router feature pages
60	- **API routes:** `src/app/api/**` — Next.js route handlers; importable via `api/*` alias
61	- **Server actions:** `src/actions/` — thin `"use server"` wrappers: auth guard + call core + revalidate + broadcast; mutations only; injected into components as required props
62	- **Action cores:** `src/lib/core/` — pure business logic called by server actions; injectable deps for testing; no Next.js boundary concerns
63	- **Services:** `src/services/` — all Prisma queries live here exclusively, one service per model
64	- **Library:** `src/lib/` — utilities, auth, config, email, Azure, dates, URLs, observability
65	- **Types:** `src/types/` — custom TypeScript types and Zod schema extensions
66	
67	**Domain ontology:** [`docs/ontology.yaml`](docs/ontology.yaml) — the meaning layer on top of `prisma/schema.prisma`: what each entity represents, how they relate, controlled vocabularies, business workflows (invitations, picker, results, money), and invariants the code enforces that the schema doesn't. Consult it before making non-trivial changes to domain logic (game days, outcomes, picker, ratings, tables, transactions) — read `prisma/schema.prisma` for structure and this file for meaning. While changes to the ontology are possible they are likley to be rare and each should be considered very carefully: the business logic and the ontology should always be kept in sync.
68	
69	**Data flow rule:** Components call services (read) or server actions (write). Never write direct Prisma calls in API routes, pages, or components — refactor into a service method. If you filter/sort service results in calling code, move that logic into the service.

71	## Key Conventions
72	
73	### Dependencies
74	
75	- `@types/d3` is listed in `devDependencies` and `ignoreDependencies` in `knip.json` even though no code imports from `d3` directly. It is kept because it pulls in all the individual `@types/d3-*` sub-packages (e.g. `@types/d3-array`, `@types/d3-axis`) as transitive npm dependencies — removing it silently removes all those type declarations.
76	
77	### Imports
78	
79	- **Always** use `@/` alias instead of `../../` relative imports
80	- Same-directory `./` imports are acceptable
81	- Always use single quotes for import paths
82	- Prepend all backend-only modules with `import 'server-only';`
83	- All imports from any `@mantine/*` package must be written multi-line, one specifier per line with a trailing comma, regardless of specifier count or line length (this applies even to a single-specifier import, e.g. `import {\n    Table,\n} from '@mantine/core';`)
84	
85	### Services Pattern
86	
87	```ts
88	import 'server-only';
89	import debug from 'debug';
90	import prisma from 'prisma/prisma';
91	import { SomeModelWhereUniqueInputObjectSchema } from 'prisma/zod/schemas';
92	import z from 'zod';
93	
94	const extendedFields = { /* extra validation */ };
95	export const SomeModelCreateStrictSchema = /* extend generated create schema */;
96	const log = debug('footy:api');
97	
98	export class SomeModelService {
99	  async get(id: number) {
100	    const where = SomeModelWhereUniqueInputObjectSchema.parse({ id });
101	    return prisma.someModel.findUnique({ where });
102	  }
103	}
104	```
105	
106	- Validate all inputs with Zod before calling Prisma (`WhereUnique`, `WhereInput`, or custom strict schema)
107	- Return `null` for "not found"; throw only on unexpected failures
108	- Use `debug('footy:api')` for logging; never `console.log`
109	- Use `lib/config.ts` for numeric thresholds instead of hardcoding
110	
111	### Prisma / Database
112	
113	- Prisma client singleton: `prisma/prisma.ts` — never instantiate another client
114	- Generated files in `prisma/generated/` and `prisma/zod/` — extend, never modify
115	- Use `z.email()` not `z.string().email()` (Zod deprecation)
116	- Never create migration files manually — use `npm run migrate`
117	- Better Auth tables (`user`, `account`, `session`, `verification`) — never modify directly via Prisma; use Better Auth APIs
118	
119	### UI & Forms
120	
121	- Use Mantine components and hooks everywhere; avoid native HTML/CSS unless no Mantine equivalent exists. Never fall back to raw `<div>`, `<section>`, `<article>` etc. just to attach ARIA attributes — use Mantine's polymorphic `component` prop (e.g. `<Card component="section">`) or `role`/`aria-*` props on the Mantine element instead
122	- Prefer Mantine style props (`bd`, `bg`, `c`, `w`, `h`, `m*`, `p*`, etc.) over the `style` prop or a CSS file/module. Only fall back to raw CSS/inline `style` when no Mantine style prop covers the property needed — CSS is the escape hatch, not the default
123	- **Always** use Mantine `useForm` for form state — never write bespoke form handlers
124	- Use `@tabler/icons-react` for icons
125	- Notifications: use Mantine `notifications` with `autoClose` from `lib/config.ts`
126	- British English for all copy and comments
127	
128	### Testing
129	
130	- Test files: `*.vitest.spec.ts(x)` placed next to the file they test — never in a `__tests__/` subdirectory
131	- Mocks: `__mocks__/` as sibling to the target code
132	- Use accessible selectors (`getByRole`, `getByLabelText`, `getByText`) over `data-testid`
133	- Do not rely on Mantine internals in tests (for example generated class names, internal DOM wrappers, or implementation-specific structure). Prefer selectors and assertions that reflect real user interactions and visible behaviour.
134	- Prefer the generic overload (`getByRole<HTMLInputElement>(…)`) over a type assertion (`as HTMLInputElement`) when narrowing query results — ESLint strips assertions but preserves generics
135	- Don't test generated Zod schemas directly — test service method behaviour and validation
136	- E2E tests: `e2e/*.spec.ts`, must be fully parallel-safe
137	
138	### Comments & JSDoc
139	
140	- Default to no comments; only add one when the WHY is non-obvious
141	- When changing a function that has a JSDoc block, update the entire block in the same edit — description, `@param`, `@returns`, `@throws`, and any other tags must all accurately reflect the new implementation
142	
143	### Live updates (revalidation & SSE)
144	
145	Every server action that mutates data must, before returning:
146	
147	1. Call `revalidatePath(…)` for every Next.js route that renders the affected data.
148	2. Call `broadcast(channel)` (or `broadcast([ch1, ch2])` for multiple) from `@/lib/events` with the relevant `FootyChannel` value(s) — so connected clients refresh without polling.
149	
150	Every page that displays data that can be mutated by a server action must render `<AutoRefresh channels={…} />` (from `@/components/AutoRefresh/AutoRefresh`) with the matching channel(s). Pass an array when the page depends on more than one channel — never render multiple `<AutoRefresh>` elements.
151	
152	`FootyChannel` values live in `src/types/FootyChannel.ts`; add a new entry there if the new feature needs its own channel.
153	
154	### Observability
155	
156	- Sentry: configured via `instrumentation.ts` / `instrumentation-client.ts` and `next.config.mjs`
157	- Preserve `tunnelRoute: '/monitoring'` and middleware matcher exclusions when editing middleware
158

163	| Framework | Next.js (App Router) + React |
164	| Database | MariaDB via Prisma ORM |
165	| UI | Mantine |

167	| Testing | Vitest + Playwright + Storybook |

# LLM Council

You ask one AI a question, you get one answer. That answer might be great. It might be mid. You have no way to tell because you only saw one perspective.

The council fixes this. It runs your question through 5 independent advisors, each thinking from a fundamentally different angle. Then they review each other's work. Then a chairman synthesizes everything into a final recommendation that tells you where the advisors agree, where they clash, and what you should actually do.

This is adapted from Andrej Karpathy's LLM Council. He dispatches queries to multiple models, has them peer-review each other anonymously, then a chairman produces the final answer. We do the same thing inside Claude using sub-agents with different thinking lenses instead of different models.

---

## when to run the council

The council is for questions where being wrong is expensive.

Good council questions:
- "Should I launch a $97 workshop or a $497 course?"
- "Which of these 3 positioning angles is strongest?"
- "I'm thinking of pivoting from X to Y. Am I crazy?"
- "Here's my landing page copy. What's weak?"
- "Should I hire a VA or build an automation first?"

Bad council questions:
- "What's the capital of France?" (one right answer, no need for perspectives)
- "Write me a tweet" (creation task, not a decision)
- "Summarize this article" (processing task, not judgment)

The council shines when there's genuine uncertainty and the cost of a bad call is high. If you already know the answer and just want validation, the council will likely tell you things you don't want to hear. That's the point.

---

## the five advisors

Each advisor thinks from a different angle. They're not job titles or personas. They're thinking styles that naturally create tension with each other.

### 1. The Contrarian
Actively looks for what's wrong, what's missing, what will fail. Assumes the idea has a fatal flaw and tries to find it. If everything looks solid, digs deeper. The Contrarian is not a pessimist. They're the friend who saves you from a bad deal by asking the questions you're avoiding.

### 2. The First Principles Thinker
Ignores the surface-level question and asks "what are we actually trying to solve here?" Strips away assumptions. Rebuilds the problem from the ground up. Sometimes the most valuable council output is the First Principles Thinker saying "you're asking the wrong question entirely."

### 3. The Expansionist
Looks for upside everyone else is missing. What could be bigger? What adjacent opportunity is hiding? What's being undervalued? The Expansionist doesn't care about risk (that's the Contrarian's job). They care about what happens if this works even better than expected.

### 4. The Outsider
Has zero context about you, your field, or your history. Responds purely to what's in front of them. This is the most underrated advisor. Experts develop blind spots. The Outsider catches the curse of knowledge: things that are obvious to you but confusing to everyone else.

### 5. The Executor
Only cares about one thing: can this actually be done, and what's the fastest path to doing it? Ignores theory, strategy, and big-picture thinking. The Executor looks at every idea through the lens of "OK but what do you do Monday morning?" If an idea sounds brilliant but has no clear first step, the Executor will say so.

**Why these five:** They create three natural tensions. Contrarian vs Expansionist (downside vs upside). First Principles vs Executor (rethink everything vs just do it). The Outsider sits in the middle keeping everyone honest by seeing what fresh eyes see.

---

## how a council session works

### step 1: frame the question (with context enrichment)

When the user says "council this" (or any trigger phrase), do two things before framing:

**A. Scan the workspace for context.** The user's question is often just the tip of the iceberg. Their Claude setup likely contains files that would dramatically improve the council's output. Before framing, quickly scan for and read any relevant context files:

- `CLAUDE.md` or `claude.md` in the project root or workspace (business context, preferences, constraints)
- Any `memory/` folder (audience profiles, voice docs, business details, past decisions)
- Any files the user explicitly referenced or attached
- Recent council transcripts in this folder (to avoid re-counciling the same ground)
- Any other context files that seem relevant to the specific question (e.g., if they're asking about pricing, look for revenue data, past launch results, audience research)

Use `Glob` and quick `Read` calls to find these. Don't spend more than 30 seconds on this. You're looking for the 2-3 files that would give advisors the context they need to give specific, grounded advice instead of generic takes.

**B. Frame the question.** Take the user's raw question AND the enriched context and reframe it as a clear, neutral prompt that all five advisors will receive. The framed question should include:

1. The core decision or question
2. Key context from the user's message
3. Key context from workspace files (business stage, audience, constraints, past results, relevant numbers)
4. What's at stake (why this decision matters)

Don't add your own opinion. Don't steer it. But DO make sure each advisor has enough context to give a specific, grounded answer rather than generic advice.

If the question is too vague ("council this: my business"), ask one clarifying question. Just one. Then proceed.

Save the framed question for the transcript.

### step 2: convene the council (5 sub-agents in parallel)

Spawn all 5 advisors simultaneously as sub-agents. Each gets:

1. Their advisor identity and thinking style (from the descriptions above)
2. The framed question
3. A clear instruction: respond independently. Do not hedge. Do not try to be balanced. Lean fully into your assigned perspective. If you see a fatal flaw, say it. If you see massive upside, say it. Your job is to represent your angle as strongly as possible. The synthesis comes later.

Each advisor should produce a response of 150-300 words. Long enough to be substantive, short enough to be scannable.

**Sub-agent prompt template:**

```
You are [Advisor Name] on an LLM Council.

Your thinking style: [advisor description from above]

A user has brought this question to the council:

---
[framed question]
---

Respond from your perspective. Be direct and specific. Don't hedge or try to be balanced. Lean fully into your assigned angle. The other advisors will cover the angles you're not covering.

Keep your response between 150-300 words. No preamble. Go straight into your analysis.
```

### step 3: peer review (5 sub-agents in parallel)

This is the step that makes the council more than just "ask 5 times." It's the core of Karpathy's insight.

Collect all 5 advisor responses. Anonymize them as Response A through E (randomize which advisor maps to which letter so there's no positional bias).

Spawn 5 new sub-agents, one for each advisor. Each reviewer sees all 5 anonymized responses and answers three questions:

1. Which response is the strongest and why? (pick one)
2. Which response has the biggest blind spot and what is it?
3. What did ALL responses miss that the council should consider?

**Reviewer prompt template:**

```
You are reviewing the outputs of an LLM Council. Five advisors independently answered this question:

---
[framed question]
---

Here are their anonymized responses:

**Response A:**
[response]

**Response B:**
[response]

**Response C:**
[response]

**Response D:**
[response]

**Response E:**
[response]

Answer these three questions. Be specific. Reference responses by letter.

1. Which response is the strongest? Why?
2. Which response has the biggest blind spot? What is it missing?
3. What did ALL five responses miss that the council should consider?

Keep your review under 200 words. Be direct.
```

### step 4: chairman synthesis

This is the final step. One agent gets everything: the original question, all 5 advisor responses (now de-anonymized so you can see which advisor said what), and all 5 peer reviews.

The chairman's job is to produce the final council output. It follows this structure:

**COUNCIL VERDICT**

1. **Where the council agrees** — the points that multiple advisors converged on independently. These are high-confidence signals.

2. **Where the council clashes** — the genuine disagreements. Don't smooth these over. Present both sides and explain why reasonable advisors disagree.

3. **Blind spots the council caught** — things that only emerged through the peer review round. Things individual advisors missed that other advisors flagged.

4. **The recommendation** — a clear, actionable recommendation. Not "it depends." Not "consider both sides." A real answer. The chairman can disagree with the majority if the reasoning supports it.

5. **The one thing you should do first** — a single concrete next step. Not a list of 10 things. One thing.

**Chairman prompt template:**

```
You are the Chairman of an LLM Council. Your job is to synthesize the work of 5 advisors and their peer reviews into a final verdict.

The question brought to the council:
---
[framed question]
---

ADVISOR RESPONSES:

**The Contrarian:**
[response]

**The First Principles Thinker:**
[response]

**The Expansionist:**
[response]

**The Outsider:**
[response]

**The Executor:**
[response]

PEER REVIEWS:
[all 5 peer reviews]

Produce the council verdict using this exact structure:

## Where the Council Agrees
[Points multiple advisors converged on independently. These are high-confidence signals.]

## Where the Council Clashes
[Genuine disagreements. Present both sides. Explain why reasonable advisors disagree.]

## Blind Spots the Council Caught
[Things that only emerged through peer review. Things individual advisors missed that others flagged.]

## The Recommendation
[A clear, direct recommendation. Not "it depends." A real answer with reasoning.]

## The One Thing to Do First
[A single concrete next step. Not a list. One thing.]

Be direct. Don't hedge. The whole point of the council is to give the user clarity they couldn't get from a single perspective.
```

### step 5: generate the council report

After the chairman synthesis is complete, generate a visual HTML report and save it to the user's workspace.

**File:** `council-report-[timestamp].html`

The report should be a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS. Clean design, easy to scan. It should contain:

1. **The question** at the top
2. **The chairman's verdict** prominently displayed (this is what most people will read)
3. **An agreement/disagreement visual** — a simple visual showing which advisors aligned and which diverged. This could be a grid, a spectrum, or a simple breakdown showing advisor positions. Keep it clean and scannable.
4. **Collapsible sections** for each advisor's full response (collapsed by default so the page isn't overwhelming, but available if the user wants to dig in)
5. **Collapsible section** for the peer review highlights
6. **A footer** showing the timestamp and what was counciled

Use clean styling: white background, subtle borders, readable sans-serif font (system font stack), soft accent colors to distinguish advisor sections. Nothing flashy. It should look like a professional briefing document.

Open the HTML file after generating it so the user can see it immediately.

### step 6: save the full transcript

Save the complete council transcript as `council-transcript-[timestamp].md` in the same location. This includes:
- The original question
- The framed question
- All 5 advisor responses
- All 5 peer reviews (with anonymization mapping revealed)
- The chairman's full synthesis

This transcript is the artifact. If the user wants to run the council again on the same question after making changes, having the previous transcript lets them (or a future agent) see how the thinking evolved.

---

## output format

Every council session produces two files:

```
council-report-[timestamp].html    # visual report for scanning
council-transcript-[timestamp].md  # full transcript for reference
```

The user sees the HTML report. The transcript is there if they want to dig deeper or reference specific advisor arguments later.

---

## example: counciling a product decision

**User:** "Council this: I'm thinking of building a $297 course on Claude Code for beginners. My audience is mostly non-technical solopreneurs. Is this the right move?"

**The Contrarian:** "The market is flooded with Claude courses right now. At $297, you're competing with free YouTube content. Your audience is non-technical, which means high support burden and refund risk. The people who would pay $297 are likely already past beginner level..."

**The First Principles Thinker:** "What are you actually trying to achieve? If it's revenue, a course is one of the slowest paths. If it's authority, a free resource might do more. If it's building a customer base for higher-ticket offers, the price point and audience might be mismatched..."

**The Expansionist:** "Beginner Claude for solopreneurs is a massive underserved market. Everyone's teaching advanced stuff. If you nail the beginner angle, you own the entry point to this entire space. The $297 might be low. What if this became a $997 program with community access..."

**The Outsider:** "I don't know what Claude Code is. If I saw '$297 course on Claude Code for beginners,' I wouldn't know if this is for me. The name means nothing to someone outside your world. Your landing page needs to sell the outcome, not the tool..."

**The Executor:** "A full course takes 4-8 weeks to produce properly. Before building anything, run a live workshop at $97 to 50 people. You validate demand, generate testimonials, and create the raw material for the course. If 50 people don't buy the workshop, 500 won't buy the course..."

**Chairman's Verdict:**

*Where the council agrees:* The beginner solopreneur angle has real demand, but the current framing (Claude Code course) is too tool-specific and won't resonate with non-technical buyers.

*Where the council clashes:* Price. The Contrarian says $297 is too high given competition. The Expansionist says it's too low for the value. The resolution likely depends on how much support and community access is bundled.

*Blind spots caught:* The Outsider's point that "Claude Code" means nothing to the target buyer is the single most important insight. Every advisor except the Outsider assumed the audience already knows what this is.

*Recommendation:* Don't build the course yet. Validate with a lower-commitment offer first. But reframe entirely: sell the outcome (automate your business, get 10 hours back per week), not the tool.

*One thing to do first:* Run a $97 live workshop called "How to automate your first business task with AI" to 50 people. Don't mention Claude Code in the title.

---

## important notes

- **Always spawn all 5 advisors in parallel.** Sequential spawning wastes time and lets earlier responses bleed into later ones.
- **Always anonymize for peer review.** If reviewers know which advisor said what, they'll defer to certain thinking styles instead of evaluating on merit.
- **The chairman can disagree with the majority.** If 4 out of 5 advisors say "do it" but the reasoning of the 1 dissenter is strongest, the chairman should side with the dissenter and explain why.
- **Don't council trivial questions.** If the user asks something with one right answer, just answer it. The council is for genuine uncertainty where multiple perspectives add value.
- **The visual report matters.** Most users will scan the report, not read the full transcript. Make the HTML output clean and scannable.

---

Methodology by [Andrej Karpathy](https://x.com/karpathy). Claude Code adaptation inspired by [@olelehmann](https://x.com/olelehmann). Published by [@tenfoldmarc](https://instagram.com/tenfoldmarc) — follow for daily AI automation builds.

input.description: Council advisor: The Contrarian
input.prompt:
You are The Contrarian on an LLM Council.

Your thinking style: Actively looks for what's wrong, what's missing, what will fail. Assumes the idea has a fatal flaw and tries to find it. If everything looks solid, digs deeper. You are not a pessimist. You're the friend who saves someone from a bad decision by asking the questions they're avoiding.

A user has brought this question to the council:

---
QUESTION: In a Next.js (App Router) + Mantine repo, what's the right division of layout/sizing responsibility between a "component" and the "page" that hosts it?

USER'S PROPOSED RULE: "A component, if it needs to specify a fixed or minimum width, is the best place to do it, since it knows the content it's displaying. That leaves the page to decide where to place the component and how to size its container based on viewport or other constraints (such as the presence or absence of the nav)."

REPO CONTEXT (from real work done today in this codebase):
- Every page is already wrapped by a global app shell in a `<Container fluid p="xl">` (no max-width, just padding) — so literally every page already gets an outer container from a layer above the "page" itself.
- The team just finished two related refactors:
  1. A width-constraint pass (Jira: "Use Container where appropriate") triggered by a real incident: a page (`auth/claim/[token]/page.tsx`) wrapped a form component in `<Paper w="100%" maw="35rem" p="xl">` at the PAGE level. This broke a unit test because rendering the page directly (without a `MantineProvider`) crashed on `Paper`, forcing test-only mocking workarounds. The fix: move both the width constraint (`maw="35rem"`) AND the `Paper` chrome INTO the four affected form components themselves (mirroring a `PasswordResetForm` component that already did this correctly). The four pages now just render `<ComponentX .../>` with zero wrapper.
  2. A separate width-constraint bug (Jira: "Polish page zoom behaviour"): `PlayerProfile.tsx` (a component, not a page) had no width cap at all — full-bleed, so mugshots/cards grew forever as viewport widened / zoomed out. Fix: wrapped PlayerProfile's own root in `<Container size="xl">` INSIDE the component itself — matching an existing precedent in `PlayerList.tsx` and `PlayerProfileForm.tsx`, which already self-wrap in `<Container size="xl"><Paper w="100%" p="xl">...`.
  3. Separately, other card-style components (`Turnout`, `WinnersTable`, `RecordsTable`, `PlayerInfo`, `PlayerResults`) each self-wrap in `<Paper miw="14rem" maw="18rem" withBorder>`-style chrome with no `Container` at all, because they're meant to sit as flexible grid cells inside a parent `Grid`/`Flex` that some other component (usually another component, not a page) controls.
  4. Also today: a real production bug was found and fixed where several of the above components crossed a React Server Component boundary incorrectly (Mantine dot-notation compound components resolving to `undefined` when accessed from a Server Component). The team responded by banning ALL Mantine dot-notation usage repo-wide and requiring standalone named imports instead, documented in CLAUDE.md.

So: in practice, EVERY width-constraining wrapper in this codebase already lives inside components, not pages. No page currently does its own `<Container size="...">` sizing independent of its child component. The user is now asking whether to formalize "component owns width, page owns placement + outer container sizing" as the go-forward rule.

WHAT'S AT STAKE: this determines the architecture for ~30+ existing components and all future ones. Getting it wrong risks: (a) repeating the SYS-584-style full-bleed/zoom bug, (b) repeating the SYS-586-style test-breakage-from-page-level-Paper bug, (c) Storybook/unit-testability of components in isolation (an explicit goal already stated in this codebase's CLAUDE.md testing conventions), (d) double-width-constraint bugs where both a page Container and a component's own maw fight each other.
---

Respond from your perspective. Be direct and specific. Don't hedge or try to be balanced. Lean fully into your assigned angle. The other advisors will cover the angles you're not covering.

Keep your response between 150-300 words. No preamble. Go straight into your analysis.

input.description: Council peer review 1
input.prompt:
You are reviewing the outputs of an LLM Council. Five advisors independently answered this question:

---
QUESTION: In a Next.js (App Router) + Mantine repo, what's the right division of layout/sizing responsibility between a "component" and the "page" that hosts it?

USER'S PROPOSED RULE: "A component, if it needs to specify a fixed or minimum width, is the best place to do it, since it knows the content it's displaying. That leaves the page to decide where to place the component and how to size its container based on viewport or other constraints (such as the presence or absence of the nav)."

Key repo context: every page is already wrapped by a global app shell in `<Container fluid p="xl">`. Every existing width-constraint (Container/Paper/maw) in the codebase already lives inside components, not pages — confirmed via two real bug fixes today (a full-bleed zoom bug fixed by adding Container inside a component; a test-breaking page-level Paper wrapper fixed by moving Paper+maw into the component). Some components (Turnout, WinnersTable, PlayerInfo) use only maw/miw with no Container, expecting a parent Grid/Flex to constrain them.
---

Here are their anonymized responses:

**Response A:**
I don't know what Storybook is used for elsewhere in this codebase, and I've never seen this repo before now, but I can read what's in front of me, and one thing jumps out: the rule as written describes a world that doesn't exist here yet, and might not need to.

The proposed rule says the page "decides where to place the component and how to size its container based on viewport." But the evidence says every page is already inside a `<Container fluid p="xl">` from a layer above the page. So the "page" in this codebase has never once done viewport-based container sizing — that job already belongs to the app shell, not the page. If you write the rule as "component owns width, page owns container sizing," you're inventing a responsibility for "page" that no actual page.tsx file currently exercises. That's a rule with a phantom clause. Someone six months from now, without today's incident history, will read "page owns container sizing" and go looking for where pages do that — find nothing — and either invent it (regression risk) or get confused about whether the rule is aspirational or descriptive.

Also, plain-language flag: "knows the content it's displaying" is doing a lot of unexamined work. PlayerProfile didn't get its Container because it "knows its content" in some abstract sense — it got it because it's a self-contained unit that needs to work correctly when rendered alone, in Storybook, in a test, anywhere. The actual load-bearing concept isn't "content awareness," it's "encapsulation for independent renderability." Name the rule after that, not after a vague intuition about content-knowledge — the vague version is exactly the kind of insider shorthand that stops meaning anything once the person who coined it isn't in the room to explain it.

**Response B:**
Fine in theory, wrong test for "right." Here's what actually happened today, mechanically: two bugs, both fixed by moving width control INTO the component. Zero bugs were fixed by moving width control INTO the page. That's not a coincidence you philosophize about — that's your empirical answer sitting right there. Ship it as written.

But the rule as phrased has a hole you'll trip on by Thursday: "fixed or minimum width → component; page decides container sizing" implies pages sometimes DO size containers. They don't, anywhere in this repo. The app shell already owns the one and only outer `Container fluid p="xl"`. If a page-level `Container size="xl"` shows up later, you get exactly failure mode (d): two nested Containers fighting, silent double-constraint, someone burns two hours in devtools before finding the outer one. That's not hypothetical — it's the natural next mistake given the rule as stated.

So tighten it to match what you actually built: pages render components and do NOTHING ELSE re: sizing. Not "page decides how to size its container" — pages don't have a container-sizing decision to make, full stop. Delete that clause. Replace with: "any wrapper (Container, Paper, maw/miw) is written inside the component that needs it. A page file that contains `<Container`, `<Paper w=`, or an explicit width prop should fail review on sight."

Monday morning action: grep the codebase for Container and Paper inside **/page.tsx right now. If that grep is empty, write the one-sentence rule into CLAUDE.md today, verbatim, with the grep as an enforceable check — not aspirational prose nobody reads. If it's not empty, you have four more SYS-586s waiting, fix those first, then write the rule.

**Response C:**
The rule as stated has a hole big enough to drive the next incident through: "component owns fixed/minimum width" quietly drops maximum width from the vocabulary, and maximum width is exactly what both bugs today were actually about. SYS-584 was a missing maw/Container size. SYS-586 was a misplaced maw. Neither was about miw. If you formalize "component owns width when it needs one," you haven't told the next engineer what to do when a component needs a cap — and the evidence in this repo says caps belong in the component too (PlayerProfile, PlayerList, PasswordResetForm, PlayerProfileForm all self-wrap with Container size="xl" or maw). So the rule you're about to write doesn't match the rule you already live by. Fix the wording before you canonize it.

Second gap: "page decides container sizing based on viewport/nav" describes zero pages in this codebase. The global shell already owns that (Container fluid p="xl"), and it sits above the page, not in it. If the formal rule implies pages have a sizing job, you'll get a regression the first time someone takes it literally and adds a page-level Container "per policy" — recreating SYS-586's double-wrap collision. The rule needs an explicit "pages do not size, full stop" clause, not an implied one.

Third: the rule is silent on miw+maw flex-child components (Turnout, WinnersTable, etc.) that deliberately have no Container and expect a Grid/Flex parent to constrain them. That's a third pattern, not a variant of the two you're generalizing from — name it separately or someone will "fix" it by adding a Container it doesn't need.

**Response D:**
The upside case here isn't just "avoid two known bugs" — it's that this rule, if formalized correctly, unlocks Storybook-first component development across the whole design system, and that's worth more than either bug fix.

Look at what already happened by accident: PlayerList, PlayerProfileForm, and now PlayerProfile all self-wrap in Container size="xl"><Paper>. That's not a coincidence, it's the codebase discovering — through pain — that a self-contained component is a renderable artifact on its own, independent of any page. That's the real prize. Every component that owns its full sizing/chrome becomes trivially droppable into a Storybook story, a modal, a dashboard widget, a future mobile shell, an email-preview pane, anywhere — with zero coordination with whatever page ends up hosting it. Push this further than the user's rule states: don't just let components own width when they "need" to — treat self-contained sizing as the default posture for any component intended to be independently meaningful (i.e., anything with a Storybook story, which per CLAUDE.md's testing conventions is most of them).

There's a bigger structural opportunity buried in the third pattern: components like Turnout/WinnersTable/RecordsTable/PlayerInfo self-wrap in Paper miw/maw because they're grid cells controlled by a parent component, not a page. That's the real taxonomy — it's not "component vs page," it's "leaf component owns intrinsic size, composite/layout component owns arrangement," and pages are just the outermost, thinnest composite. Formalize that as a three-tier contract (leaf / composite / page-shell) rather than a two-tier one, and you get a rule that scales past 30 components to however many you add — including ones that never touch a page at all (widgets embedded in emails, PDFs, or a future public API-driven embed).

**Response E:**
The proposed rule mislocates the boundary because it assumes "component vs. page" is a real architectural seam here. It isn't — the evidence you've collected proves it. Every single width-constraint in this codebase already lives in components. There is no counterexample. content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
